title: Flowering stage management — controlled evidence plan
purpose: Define flowering transition, photoperiod verification, reproductive scouting, environment/load monitoring and late-flower risk controls without universal flowering recipes.

excludedUntilValidated: assumption that one photoperiod response fits all genotypes
ignoring intersex findings because plants were feminized
harvest release based on calendar date alone

claims.statement: Cannabis flowering development is shaped by genotype, photoperiod and environment, so flowering-stage management should preserve actual developmental observations alongside programmed schedules.
claims.boundary: A programmed light schedule does not prove identical developmental timing across genotypes.

claims.statement: Photoperiod and uninterrupted dark-period control are important flowering variables, supporting verification of actual timer/controller operation and light-leak or schedule deviations.
claims.boundary: The course should not convert one research treatment into a universal flowering schedule for all cannabis genetics.

claims.statement: Unexpected male or intersex reproductive structures can occur in cannabis and may have genetic, hormonal, developmental and environmental contributors, so reproductive scouting and escalation should continue during flowering.
claims.boundary: No single stress trigger should be treated as a universal explanation for all intersex expression.

claims.statement: As canopy and inflorescence biomass increase, moisture and heat loads and within-canopy gradients can change, requiring representative environmental monitoring rather than reliance on controller averages alone.
claims.boundary: Research temperature/RH/VPD values are evidence of relationships, not universal flowering setpoints.

claims.statement: Trichome and inflorescence maturation are asynchronous and genotype-dependent, so late-flower tracking should combine representative observations with the defined harvest objective instead of using one visual rule.
claims.boundary: Trichome color or flowering week alone does not directly establish cannabinoid concentration or whole-lot readiness.

claims.statement: Late-flower management should preserve pest/disease, reproductive, environmental and irrigation deviations because quality and harvest decisions depend on the crop's actual history, not only its final appearance.
claims.boundary: A visually mature crop does not automatically clear an unresolved plant-health or quality hold.
